entries.fc5830b96eda07494f8987e69ea7e79394af852b: <div sID="gen20862" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Zech.7" sID="Zech.7"/> <div eID="gen20862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20863" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20864" type="x-p"/> We have done with the visions, but not with the revelations of this book; the prophet sees no more such signs as he had seen, but still "the word of the Lord came to him." In this chapter we have, I. A case of conscience proposed to the prophet by the children of the captivity concerning fasting, whether they should continue their solemn fasts which they had religiously observed during the seventy years of their captivity, <reference osisRef="Zech.7.1-Zech.7.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The answer to this question, which is given in this and the next chapter; and this answer was given not all at once, but by piece-meal, and, it should seem, at several times, for here are four distinct discourses which have all of them reference to this case, each of them prefaced with "the word of the Lord came," <reference osisRef="Zech.4.8 Zech.8.1 Zech.8.18">ver. 4-8 and ch. viii. 1, 18</reference>. The method of them is very observable. In this chapter, 1. The prophet sharply reproves them for the mismanagements of their fasts, <reference osisRef="Zech.7.4-Zech.7.7">ver. 4-7</reference>. 2. He exhorts them to reform their lives, which would be the best way of fasting, and to take heed of those sins which brought those judgments upon them which they kept these fasts in memory of, <reference osisRef="Zech.7.8-Zech.7.14">ver. 8-14</reference>. And then in the next chapter, having searched the wound, he binds it up, and heals it, with gracious assurances of great mercy God had yet in store for them, by which he would turn their fasts into feasts.
entries.066fbc8282a772c74732950e3142381d6f1e73a4: <div eID="gen20864" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20863" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">An Enquiry Concerning Fasting; Hypocrisy Reproved. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20865" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass in the fourth year of king Darius, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto Zechariah in the fourth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the ninth month, <hi type="italic">even</hi> in Chisleu; <hi type="super">2</hi> When they had sent unto the house of God Sherezer and Regem-melech, and their men, to pray before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="italic">And</hi> to speak unto the priests which <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, and to the prophets, saying, Should I weep in the fifth month, separating myself, as I have done these so many years? <hi type="super">4</hi> Then came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts unto me, saying, <hi type="super">5</hi> Speak unto all the people of the land, and to the priests, saying, When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh <hi type="italic">month,</hi> even those seventy years, did ye at all fast unto me, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to me? <hi type="super">6</hi> And when ye did eat, and when ye did drink, did not ye eat <hi type="italic">for yourselves,</hi> and drink <hi type="italic">for yourselves?</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="italic">Should ye</hi> not <hi type="italic">hear</hi> the words which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath cried by the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and in prosperity, and the cities thereof round about her, when <hi type="italic">men</hi> inhabited the south and the plain? <div eID="gen20865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20866" type="x-p"/> This occasional sermon, which the prophet preached, and which is recorded in this and the next chapter, was above two years after the former, in which he gave them an account of his visions, as appears by comparing the date of this (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.1">v. 1</reference>), in the <hi type="italic">ninth month</hi> of the <hi type="italic">fourth year</hi> of Darius, with the date of that (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.1">ch. i. 1</reference>), in the eighth month of the second year of Darius; not that Zechariah was idle all that while (it is expressly said that he and Haggai continued <hi type="italic">prophesying</hi> till the temple was finished in the sixth year of Darius; <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.14-Ezra.6.15">Ezra vi. 14, 15</reference>), but during that time he did not preach any sermon that was afterwards published, and left upon record, as this is. God may be honoured, his work done, and his interest served, by word of mouth as well as by writing; and by inculcating and pressing what has been taught, as well as by advancing something new. Now here we have, <div eID="gen20866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20867" type="x-p"/> I. A case proposed concerning fasting. Some persons were sent to enquire of the priests and prophets whether they should continue to observe their yearly fasts, particularly that in the fifth month, as they had done. It is uncertain whether the case was put by those that yet remained in Babylon, who, being deprived of the benefit of the solemn feasts which God's ordinance appointed them, made up the want by the solemn fasts which God's providences called them to; or by those that had returned, but lived in the country, as some rather incline to think, because they are called the <hi type="italic">people of the land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.7.5">v. 5</reference>. But, as to that, the answer given to the messengers of the captive Jews might be directed, not to them only, but to <hi type="italic">all the people.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen20867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20868" type="x-p"/> 1. Who they were that came with this enquiry—<hi type="italic">Sherezer</hi> and <hi type="italic">Regem-melech,</hi> persons of some rank and figure, for they came <hi type="italic">with their men,</hi> and did not think it below them, or any disparagement to them, to be sent on this errand, but rather an addition to their honour to be, (1.) Attendants in God's house, there to do duty and receive orders. The greatest of men are less than the least of the ordinances of Jesus Christ. (2.) Agents for God's people, to negotiate their affairs. Men of estates, having more leisure than men of business, ought to employ their time in the service of the public, and by doing good they make themselves truly great; the <hi type="italic">messengers of the churches</hi> were the <hi type="italic">glory of Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.23">2 Cor. viii. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen20868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20869" type="x-p"/> 2. What the errand was upon which they came. They were sent perhaps not with <hi type="italic">gold and silver</hi> (as those, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.10-Zech.6.11">ch. vi. 10, 11</reference>), or, if they were, that is not mentioned, but upon the two great errands which should bring us all to the house of God, (1.) to intercede with God for his mercy. They were sent to <hi type="italic">pray before the Lord,</hi> and, some think (according to the usage then), to <hi type="italic">offer sacrifice,</hi> with which they offered up their prayers. The Jews, in captivity, prayed towards the temple (as appears <reference osisRef="Dan.6.10">Dan. vi. 10</reference>); but now that it was in a fair way to be rebuilt they sent their representatives to pray in it, remembering that God had said that his house should be called <hi type="italic">a house of prayer for all people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.56.7">Isa. lvi. 7</reference>. In prayer we must set ourselves as <hi type="italic">before the Lord,</hi> must see his eye upon us and have our eye up to him. (2.) To enquire of God concerning his mind. Note, When we offer up our requests to God it must be with a readiness to receive instructions from him; for, if we turn away our ear from hearing his law, we cannot expect that our prayers should be acceptable to him. We must therefore desire to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of our life <hi type="italic">that we may enquire</hi> there (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Ps. xxvii. 4</reference>), asking, not only, Lord, what wilt thou do for me? but, Lord <hi type="italic">what wilt thou have me to do?</hi> <div eID="gen20869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20870" type="x-p"/> 3. Whom they consulted. They spoke <hi type="italic">to the priests that were in the house of the Lord and to the prophets;</hi> the former were an oracle for ordinary cases, the latter for extraordinary; they were blessed with both, and would try if either could acquaint them with the mind of God in this case. Note, God having given diversities of gifts to men, and all to profit with, we should make use of all as there is occasion. They were not so wedded to the priests, their stated ministers, as to distrust the prophets, who appeared, by the gifts given them, well qualified to serve the church; nor yet were they so much enamoured with the prophets as to despise the priests, but they spoke both to the priests and to the prophets, and, in consulting both, gave glory to the God of Israel, and that one Spirit who <hi type="italic">works all in all.</hi> God might speak to them either by <hi type="italic">urim</hi> or <hi type="italic">by prophets</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.6">1 Sam. xxviii. 6</reference>), and therefore they would not neglect either. The priests and the prophets were not jealous one of another, nor had any difference among themselves; let not the people then make differences between them, but thank God they had both. The prophets did indeed reprove what was amiss in the priests, but at the same time told the people that the <hi type="italic">priest's lips</hi> should <hi type="italic">keep knowledge,</hi> and they must <hi type="italic">enquire the law at his mouth,</hi> for <hi type="italic">he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.7">Mal. ii. 7</reference>. Note, Those that would know God's mind should consult God's ministers, and in doubtful cases ask advice of those whose special business it is to <hi type="italic">search the scriptures.</hi> <div eID="gen20870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20871" type="x-p"/> 4. What the case was which they desired satisfaction in (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Should I weep in the fifth month, separating myself, as I have done these so many years.</hi> Observe, (1.) What had been their past practice, not only during the seventy years of the captivity but to this time, which was twenty years after the liberty proclaimed them; they kept up solemn stated fasts for humiliation and prayer, which they religiously observed, according as their opportunities were, in their closets, families, or such assemblies for worship as they had. In the case here, they mention only one, that of the fifth month; but it appears, by <reference osisRef="Zech.8.19">ch. viii. 19</reference>, that they observed four anniversary fasts, one in the fourth month (<hi type="italic">June</hi> 17), in remembrance of the breaking up of the wall of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.6">Jer. lii. 6</reference>), another in the fifth month (<hi type="italic">July</hi> 4), in remembrance of the burning of the temple (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.12-Jer.52.13">Jer. lii. 12, 13</reference>), another in the seventh month (<hi type="italic">September</hi> 3), in remembrance of the killing of Gedaliah, which completed their dispersion, and another in the tenth month (<hi type="italic">December</hi> 10), in remembrance of the beginning of the siege of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1">2 Kings xxv. 1</reference>. Now it was very commendable in them to keep those fasts, thus to humble themselves under those humbling providences, by which God called them to weeping and mourning, thus to accommodate themselves to their troubles, and prepare themselves for deliverance. It would likewise be a means of possessing their children betimes with a due sense of the hand of the Lord gone out against them. (2.) What was their present doubt-whether they should continue these fasts or no. The case is put as by a single person: <hi type="italic">Should I weep?</hi> But it was the case of many, and the satisfaction of one would be a satisfaction to the rest. Or perhaps many had left it off, but the querist will not be determined by the practice of others; if God will have him continue it, he will, whatever others do. His fasting is described by his <hi type="italic">weeping, separating himself.</hi> A religious fast must be solemnized, not only by abstinence, here called a separating ourselves from the ordinary lawful comforts of life, but by a godly sorrow for sin, here expressed by weeping. "Should I still keep such <hi type="italic">days to afflict the soul</hi> as <hi type="italic">I have done these so many years?</hi>" It is said (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.5">v. 5</reference>) to be seventy years, computed from the last captivity, as before, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.12">ch. i. 12</reference>. The enquiry intimates a readiness to continue it, if God so appoint, though it be a mortification to the flesh. [1.] Something is to be said for the continuance of these fasts. Fasting and praying are good work at any time, and do good; we have always both cause enough and need enough to humble ourselves before God. To throw off these fasts would be an evidence of their being too secure, and a cause of their being more so. They were still in distress, and under the tokens of God's displeasure; and it is unwise for the patient to break off his course of physic while he is sensible of such remains of his distemper. But, [2.] There is something to be said for the letting fall of these fasts. God had changed the method of his providences concerning them, and returned in ways of mercy to them; and ought not they then to change the method of their duties? Now that the bridegroom has returned, why should the <hi type="italic">children of the bride-chamber fast?</hi> Every thing is beautiful in its season. And as to the fast of the fifth month (which is that they particularly enquire about), that, being kept in remembrance of the burning of the temple, might seem to be superseded rather than any of the other, because the temple was now in a fair way to be rebuilt. But, having long kept up this fast, they would not leave it off without advice, and without asking and knowing God's mind in the case. Note, A good method of religious services, which we have found beneficial to ourselves and others, ought not to be altered without good reason, and therefore not without mature deliberation. <div eID="gen20871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20872" type="x-p"/> II. An answer given to this case. It should seem that, though the question looked plausible enough, those who proposed it were not conscientious in it, for they were more concerned about the ceremony than about the substance; they seemed to boast of their fasting, and to upbraid God Almighty with it, that he had not sooner returned in mercy to them; "for we have done it <hi type="italic">these so many years.</hi>" As those, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.3">Isa. lviii. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">Wherefore have we fasted, and thou seest not?</hi> And some think that unbelief, and distrust of the promises of God, were at the bottom of their enquiry; for, if they had given them the credit that was due to them, they needed not to doubt but that their fasts ought to be laid aside, now that the occasion of them was over. And therefore the first answer to their enquiry is a very sharp reproof of their hypocrisy, directed, not only to the <hi type="italic">people of the land,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">the priests,</hi> who had set up these fasts, and perhaps some of them were for keeping them up, to serve some purpose of their own. Let them all take notice that, whereas they thought they had made God very much their debtor by these fasts, they were much mistaken, for they were not acceptable to him, unless they had been observed in a better manner and to better purpose. <div eID="gen20872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20873" type="x-p"/> 1. What they did that was good was not done aright (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">You fasted and mourned.</hi> They were not chargeable with the omission or neglect of the duty, though it was displeasing to the body (thy fasts were <hi type="italic">continually before me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Ps. l. 8</reference>), but they had not managed them aright. Note, Those that come to enquire of their duty must be willing first to be told of their faults. And those that seem zealous for the outside of a duty ought to examine themselves faithfully whether they have the regard they ought to have to the inside of it. (1.) They had not an eye to God in their fasting: <hi type="italic">Did you at all fast unto me, even to me?</hi> He appeals to their own consciences; they will witness against them that they had not been sincere in it, much more will God, who is greater than the heart and knows all things. You know very well that <hi type="italic">you did not at all fast to me; in fasting did you fast to me?</hi> There was the carcase and form of the duty, but none of the life, and soul, and power of it. Was it <hi type="italic">to me, even to me?</hi> The repetition intimates what a great deal of stress is laid upon this as the main matter, in that and other holy exercises, that they be done to God, even to him, with an eye to his word as our rule, and his glory as our end, in them, seeking to please him and to obtain his favour, and studious by the sincerity of our intention to approve ourselves to him. When this was wanting every fast was but a jest. To fast, and not fast to God, was to mock him and provoke him, and could not be pleasing to him. Those that make fasting a cloak for sin, as Jezebel's fast, or by it make their court to men for their applause, as the Pharisees, or that rest in outward expressions of humiliation while their hearts are unhumbled, as Ahab, do they <hi type="italic">fast to God, even to him? Is this the fast that God has chosen?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.5">Isa. lviii. 5</reference>. If the solemnities of our fasting, though frequent, long, and severe, do not serve to put an edge upon devout affections, to quicken prayer, to increase godly sorrow, and to alter the temper of our minds and the course of our lives for the better, they do not at all answer the intention, and God will not accept them as performed to him, even to him. (2.) They had the same eye to themselves in their fasting that they had in their eating and drinking (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">When you did eat, and when you did drink,</hi> on other days (nay, perhaps on your fast-days, in the observation of which you could, when you saw cause, dispense with yourselves, and take a liberty to eat and drink), did you not <hi type="italic">eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?</hi> Have you not always done as you had a mind yourselves? Why then do you now pretend a desire to know the mind of God? In your religious feasts and thanksgivings you have had no more an eye to God than in your fasts." Or, rather, it refers to their common meals; they did no more design the honour of God in their fasting and praying than they did in their eating and drinking; but self was still the centre in which the lines of all their actions, natural, civil, and religious, met. They needed not be in such care about the continuance of their fasts, unless they had kept them better. Note, We miss our end in eating and drinking when we eat to ourselves and drink to ourselves, whereas we should <hi type="italic">eat and drink to the glory of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.31">1 Cor. x. 31</reference>), that our bodies may be fit to serve our souls in his service. <div eID="gen20873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20874" type="x-p"/> 2. The principal good thing they should have done was left undone (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Should you not hear the words which the Lord has cried by the former prophets?</hi> Yes, that you should have done on your fast-days; it was not enough to <hi type="italic">weep</hi> and <hi type="italic">separate yourselves</hi> on your fast-days, in token of your sorrow for the judgments you were under, but you should have <hi type="italic">searched the scriptures</hi> of the prophets, that you might have seen what was the ground of God's controversy with your fathers, and might have taken warning by their miseries not to tread in the steps of their iniquities. You ask, Shall we do as we have done, in fasting? No, you must do that which you have not yet done; you must repent of your sins and reform you lives. This is what we now call you to, and it is the same that the former prophets called your fathers to." To affect them the more with the mischief that sin had done them, that they might be brought to repent of it, he puts them in mind of the former flourishing state of their country: Jerusalem <hi type="italic">was</hi> then <hi type="italic">inhabited and in prosperity,</hi> that is now desolate and in distress. The <hi type="italic">cities round about,</hi> that are now in ruins, were then inhabited too and <hi type="italic">in peace.</hi> The country likewise was very populous: <hi type="italic">Men inhabited the south of the plain,</hi> which was not at all fortified, and yet they lived safely, and which was fruitful, and so they lived plentifully. But then God <hi type="italic">by the prophets cried</hi> to them, as one in earnest, and importunate with them, to amend their ways and doings, or else their prosperity would soon be at an end. "Now," says the prophet, "you should have taken notice of that, and have inferred that what was required of them for the preventing of the judgments, and which they did not, is required of you for the removal of the judgments; and, if you do it not, all your fasting and weeping signify nothing." Note, The words of the later prophets agree with those of the former; and, whether people are in prosperity or adversity, they must be called upon to leave their sins and do their duty; this must still be the burden of every song.
entries.aab8cd5557a8e6509cfc4c866c9434ff06da324d: <div eID="gen20874" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Wilful Disobedience of Israel; Consequences of Disobedience. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20875" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto Zechariah, saying, <hi type="super">9</hi> Thus speaketh the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, saying, Execute true judgment, and shew mercy and compassions every man to his brother: <hi type="super">10</hi> And oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor; and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart. <hi type="super">11</hi> But they refused to hearken, and pulled away the shoulder, and stopped their ears, that they should not hear. <hi type="super">12</hi> Yea, they made their hearts <hi type="italic">as</hi> an adamant stone, lest they should hear the law, and the words which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts hath sent in his spirit by the former prophets: therefore came a great wrath from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore it is come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> as he cried, and they would not hear; so they cried, and I would not hear, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts: <hi type="super">14</hi> But I scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations whom they knew not. Thus the land was desolate after them, that no man passed through nor returned: for they laid the pleasant land desolate. <div eID="gen20875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20876" type="x-p"/> What was said <reference osisRef="Zech.7.7">v. 7</reference>, that they <hi type="italic">should have heard the words of the former prophets,</hi> is here enlarged upon, for warning to these hypocritical enquirers, who continued their sins when they asked with great preciseness whether they should continue their fasts. This prophet had before put them in mind of their fathers' disobedience to the calls of the prophets, and what was the consequence of it (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.4-Zech.1.6">ch. i. 4-6</reference>), and now here again; for others' harms should be our warnings. God's judgments upon Israel of old for their sins were written for admonition to us Christians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.11">1 Cor. x. 11</reference>), and the same use we should make of similar providences in our own day. <div eID="gen20876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20877" type="x-p"/> I. This prophet here repeats the heads of the sermons which the former prophets preached to their fathers (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.9-Zech.7.10">v. 9, 10</reference>), because the very same things were required of them now. "Thus does the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts speak</hi> to you now, and thus he did speak to your fathers, saying, <hi type="italic">Execute true judgment.</hi>" The duties here required of them, which would have been the lengthening of the tranquillity of their fathers and must be the restoring of their tranquillity, are not keeping fasts and offering sacrifices, but <hi type="italic">doing justly</hi> and <hi type="italic">loving mercy,</hi> duties which they were bound to by the light and law of nature, though there had been no prophets sent to insist upon them, duties which had a direct tendency to the public welfare and peace, and which they themselves would be the gainers by, and not God. 1. Magistrates must administer justice impartially, according to the maxims of the law and the merits of the cause, without respect of persons: "<hi type="italic">Judge judgment of truth,</hi> and execute it when you have judged it." 2. Neighbours must have a tender concern for one another, and must not only do one another no wrong, but must be ready to do one another all the good offices that lie in their power. They must <hi type="italic">show mercy and compassion every man to his brother,</hi> as the case called for it. The infirmities of others, as well as their calamities, are to be looked upon with compassion. <hi type="italic">Hanc veniam petimusque damusque vicissim—This kindness we ask and exercise.</hi> 3. They must not bear hard upon those whom they have advantage against, and who, they know, are not able to help themselves. They must not, either in commerce or in course of law, oppress <hi type="italic">the widow, the fatherless, the stranger, and the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.7.10">v. 10</reference>. The weakest must not be thrust to the wall because they are weakest. No thanks to men not to deny right to those who are in a capacity to demand it and recover it; but we must, not only for wrath, but also for conscience' sake, give those their own who have not power to force it from us. Or it intimates that that which is but exactness with others is exaction upon the widows and the fatherless; nay, that not relieving and helping them as we ought is, in effect, oppressing them. 4. They must not only not do wrong to any, but they must not so much as desire it nor think of it: "<hi type="italic">Let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart.</hi> Do not project it; do not wish it; nay do not so much as please yourself with the fancy of it." The law of God lays a restraint upon the heart, and forbids the entertaining, forbids the admitting, of a malicious, spiteful, ill-natured thought. <reference osisRef="Deut.15.9">Deut. xv. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">Beware that there be not a thought in thy Belial heart against thy brother.</hi> <div eID="gen20877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20878" type="x-p"/> II. He describes the wilfulness and disobedience of their fathers, who persisted in all manner of wickedness and injustice, notwithstanding these exhortations and admonitions frequently given them in God's name; various expressions to this purport are here heaped up (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.11-Zech.7.12">v. 11, 12</reference>), setting forth the stubbornness of that carnal mind which is <hi type="italic">enmity against God, and is not in subjection to the law of God, neither indeed can be.</hi> They were obstinate and refractory, and persisted in their transgressions of the law purely from a spirit of contradiction to the law. 1. They would not, if they could help it, come within hearing of the prophets, but kept at a distance; or, if they could not avoid hearing what they said, yet they resolved they would not heed it: <hi type="italic">They refused to hearken,</hi> and looked another way as if they had not been spoken to. 2. If they did hear what was said to them, and, as it seemed, inclined at first to comply with it, yet they flew off when it came to the setting to, and, like a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke, <hi type="italic">they pulled away the shoulder,</hi> and would not submit to the <hi type="italic">easy yoke and the light burden</hi> of God's commandments. <hi type="italic">They gave a withdrawing shoulder</hi> (so the word is); they seemed to lay their shoulder to the work, but they presently withdrew it again, as those <reference osisRef="Jer.34.10-Jer.34.11">Jer. xxxiv. 10, 11</reference>. They were like a deceitful bow, as that son that said, <hi type="italic">I go, sir, but went not.</hi> 3. They filled their own minds with prejudices against the word of God, and had some objection or other ready wherewith to fortify themselves against every sermon they heard. <hi type="italic">They stopped their ears, that they should not hear,</hi> as the deaf adder (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.4">Ps. lviii. 4</reference>), and none are so deaf as those that will not hear, that <hi type="italic">make their own ear heavy,</hi> as the word is. 4. They resolved that nothing which was said to them, for the enforcing of these injunctions, should make any impression upon them: <hi type="italic">They made their hearts as an adamant-stone,</hi> as a <hi type="italic">diamond,</hi> the hardest of stones to be wrought upon, or as a <hi type="italic">flint,</hi> which the mason cannot hew into shape as he can other stone out of the quarry. Nothing is so hard, so unmalleable, so inflexible, as the heart of a presumptuous sinner; and those whose hearts are hard may thank themselves; they are of their own hardening, and it is just with God to give them over to a reprobate sense, to the hardness and impenitence of their own hearts. These stubborn sinners hardened their hearts on purpose <hi type="italic">lest they should hear</hi> what God said to them by the written word, <hi type="italic">by the law of Moses,</hi> and by the <hi type="italic">words of the prophets</hi> that preached to them; they had <hi type="italic">Moses and the prophets,</hi> but resolved they would hear neither, nor would they have been persuaded though one had been sent to them from the dead. The <hi type="italic">words of the prophet</hi> were not regarded by them, though they were words which the Lord of hosts sent and directed to them, though he sent them immediately <hi type="italic">by his Spirit</hi> in the prophets; so that in despising them they affronted God himself and <hi type="italic">resisted the Holy Ghost.</hi> Note, The reason why men are not good is because they will not be so; they will not consider, will not comply; and therefore, <hi type="italic">if thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it.</hi> <div eID="gen20878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20879" type="x-p"/> III. He shows the fatal consequences of it to their fathers: <hi type="italic">Therefore came great wrath from the Lord of hosts.</hi> God was highly displeased with them, and justly; he required nothing of them but what was reasonable in itself and beneficial to them; and yet they refused, and in a most insolent manner too. What master could bear to be so abused by his own servant? Such an implacable enmity to the gospel as this was to the law and the prophets was that which brought <hi type="italic">wrath to the uttermost</hi> upon the last generation of the Jewish church, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.16">1 Thess. ii. 16</reference>. Great sins against <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> whose authority is incontestable, bring <hi type="italic">great wrath from the Lord of hosts,</hi> whose power is irresistible. And the effect was, 1. As they had turned a deaf ear to God's word, so God turned a deaf ear to their prayers, <reference osisRef="Zech.7.13">v. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">As he cried</hi> to them in their prosperity to leave their sins, <hi type="italic">and they would not hear,</hi> but persisted in their iniquities, so <hi type="italic">they cried to him</hi> in the day of their trouble to remove his judgments, and he would not hear, but lengthened out their calamities. Those that set God at defiance, in the height of their pride, when pangs came upon them cried unto him. <hi type="italic">Lord, in trouble have they visited thee.</hi> But God has said it, and will abide by it, <hi type="italic">He that turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be an abomination,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.9">Prov. xxviii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.24">i. 24</reference>, &c. Iniquity, regarded in the heart, will certainly spoil the success of prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Ps. lxvi. 18</reference>. 2. As they flew off from their duty and allegiance to God, and were of desultory and unsettled spirits, so God dissipated them and threw them about as chaff before a whirlwind: <hi type="italic">He scattered them among all the nations whom they knew not,</hi> and whom therefore they could not expect to receive any kindness from, <reference osisRef="Zech.7.14">v. 14</reference>. 3. As they violated all the laws of their land, so God took away all the glories of it: <hi type="italic">Their land was desolate after them, and no man passed through or returned.</hi> All that country that was the kingdom of the two tribes, after the dispersion of the remaining Jews, upon the slaughter of Gedaliah, was left utterly uninhabited; there was not man, woman, or child, in it, till the Jews returned at the end of seventy years' captivity; nay, it should seem, the very roads that lay through the country were deserted (none passed or repassed), which, as it had an intimation of mercy in it (though they were cast out of it, yet it was kept empty for their return), so for the present it made the judgment appear much the more dismal; for what a horrid wilderness must a land be that had been so many years uninhabited! And they might thank themselves; it was they that by their own wickedness laid <hi type="italic">the pleasant land desolate.</hi> It was not so much the Chaldeans that did it. No; they did it themselves. The desolations of a land are owing to the wickedness of its inhabitants, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.34">Ps. cvii. 34</reference>. This came of their wilful disobedience to the law of God. And the present generation saw how desolate sin had made that pleasant land, and yet would not take warning.  <chapter eID="Zech.7"/> <div eID="gen20879" type="x-p"/>

entries.2ca4db029fde5b4aca8f1e335476a7f7be0a0045: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13090"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.7.1-Zech.7.14">Zec 7:1-14</reference>. II. Didactic Part, Seventh and Eighth chapters. Obedience, Rather than Fasting, Enjoined: Its Reward.</title> <div sID="gen24606" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13090"/><hi type="bold">1. fourth year of ... Darius--</hi>two years after the previous prophecies (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.1">Zec 1:1</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen24606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24607" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chisleu--</hi>meaning "torpidity," the state in which nature is in November, answering to this month. <div eID="gen24607" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc5cde41cfda9d51e2db6a4b8eb90a9bf232439c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13091"/><div sID="gen24608" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13091"/><hi type="bold">2. they ... sent unto ... house of God--</hi>The Jews of the country sent to the house of God or congregation at Jerusalem. The altar was long since reared (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.3">Ezr 3:3</reference>), though the temple was not completed till two years afterwards (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.15">Ezr 6:15</reference>). The priests' duty was to give decision on points of the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.9">De 17:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.2.4">Mt 2:4</reference>). Beth-el is here used instead of Beth-Jehovah, because the religious authorities, rather than the house itself (designated "Beth-Jehovah" in <reference osisRef="Zech.7.3">Zec 7:3</reference>), are intended. The old Beth-el had long ceased to be the seat of idol-worship, so that the name had lost its opprobrious meaning. "The house of the Lord" is used for the congregation of worshippers headed by their priests (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.7">Zec 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.1">Ho 8:1</reference>). Maurer makes the "house of God" nominative to "sent." Henderson makes "Beth-el" so.<div eID="gen24608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sherezer--</hi>an Assyrian name meaning, "Prefect of the treasury."<div eID="gen24609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Regemmelech--</hi>meaning, "The king's official." These names perhaps intimate the semi-heathen character of the inquirers, which may also be implied in the name "Beth-el" (Hebrew for "house of God"), so notorious once for its calf-worship. They sent to Jehovah's house as their forefathers sent to old Beth-el, not in the spirit of true obedience.<div eID="gen24610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pray before the Lord--</hi>literally, "to entreat the face of," that is, to offer sacrifices, the accompaniment of prayers, to conciliate His favor (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.12">1Sa 13:12</reference>). <div eID="gen24611" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3d2df5d92b570f3738e5c7248e993833598bcb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13092"/><div sID="gen24612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13092"/><hi type="bold">3. Should I weep in the fifth month--</hi>"I" represents here the people of God (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.8.21">Zec 8:21</reference>). This rather favors Maurer's view, taking "the house of God," the congregation, as nominative to "sent." Their hypocrisy appeared because they showed more concern about a ceremony of human institution (not improper in itself) than about moral obedience. If, too, they had trusted God's promise as to the restoration of Church and State, the fast would have now given place to joy, for which there was more cause than for grief [Pembellus].<div eID="gen24612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the prophets--</hi>Haggai and Zechariah especially. The tenth day of the fifth month was kept a fast, being the anniversary of the destruction of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.12-Jer.52.14">Jr 52:12-14</reference>). They ask, Should the fast be continued, now that the temple and city are being restored?<div eID="gen24613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">separating myself--</hi>sanctifying myself by separation, not only from food, but from all defilements (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.2.16">Joe 2:16</reference>) as was usual in a solemn fast. <div eID="gen24614" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8f8d26c9495c4c2e587a86e8be399f5f6ab50f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13093"/><div sID="gen24615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13093"/><hi type="bold">5. Speak unto all--</hi>The question had been asked in the name of the people in general by Sherezer and Regemmelech. The self-imposed fast they were tired of, not having observed it in the spirit of true religion.<div eID="gen24615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seventh month--</hi>This fast was in memory of the murder of Gedaliah and those with him at Mizpah, issuing in the dispersion of the Jews (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.25">2Ki 25:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.1-Jer.41.3">Jr 41:1-3</reference>).<div eID="gen24616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">did ye ... fast unto me?--</hi>No; it was to gratify yourselves in hypocritical will-worship. If it had been "unto Me," ye would have "separated yourselves" not only from food, but from your sins (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.3-Isa.58.7">Is 58:3-7</reference>). They falsely made the fast an end intrinsically meritorious in itself, not a means towards God's glory in their sanctification. The true principle of piety, reference to God, was wanting: hence the emphatic repetition of "unto Me." Before settling questions as to the outward forms of piety (however proper, as in this case), the great question was as to piety itself; that being once settled, all their outward observances become sanctified, being "unto the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.6">Ro 14:6</reference>). <div eID="gen24617" type="x-p"/>
entries.666bcc7d4275a369f9490f26be183d4672a3be2c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13094"/><div sID="gen24618" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13094"/><hi type="bold">6. did not ye eat for yourselves?--</hi>literally, "Is it not ye who eat?" that is, it is not unto Me and My glory. It tends no more to My glory, your feasting than your fasting. <div eID="gen24618" type="x-p"/>
entries.aeab1ef60ee4536e41d8509ea2ed99077b2ee669: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13095"/><div sID="gen24619" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13095"/><hi type="bold">7. Should ye not hear the words--</hi>rather, "Should ye not do the words," as their question naturally was as to what they should do (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.3">Zec 7:3</reference>); "hearing" is not mentioned till <reference osisRef="Zech.7.12">Zec 7:12</reference>. The sense is, It is not fasts that Jehovah requires of you, but that ye should keep His precepts given to you at the time when Jerusalem was in its integrity. Had ye done so then, ye would have had no occasion to institute fasts to commemorate its destruction, for it would never have been destroyed (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.9-Zech.7.14">Zec 7:9-14</reference>) [Maurer]. Or, as the Margin, "Are not these the words" of the older prophets (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.3">Is 58:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.12">Jr 14:12</reference>) which threatened a curse for disobedience, which the event has so awfully confirmed. If ye follow them in sin, ye must follow them in suffering. English Version is good sense: Ye inquire anxiously about the fasts, whereas ye ought to be anxious about hearing the lesson taught by the former prophets and verified in the nation's punishment; penitence and obedience are required rather than fasts.<div eID="gen24619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the plain--</hi>southwest of Jerusalem. They then inhabited securely the region most unguarded. <div eID="gen24620" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9e2bbd067e8304a7bfe77816508cf3be3f61851: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13096"/><div sID="gen24621" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13096"/><hi type="bold">9. speaketh--</hi>implying that these precepts addressed to their ancestors were the requirements of Jehovah not merely then, but now. We must not only not hurt, but we must help our fellow men. God is pleased with such loving obedience, rather than with empty ceremonies. <div eID="gen24621" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e085e9fd584f0006eee1bfe09f2f137617e8ec8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13097"/><div sID="gen24622" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13097"/><hi type="bold">10. imagine evil--</hi>that is, devise evil. The Septuagint takes it, Harbor not the desire of revenge (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.18">Le 19:18</reference>). "Devise evil against one another" is simpler (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.4">Psa 36:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mi 2:1</reference>). <div eID="gen24622" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ffb831cf2403d9655ee2e7ff4afa44fbd5b08e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13098"/><div sID="gen24623" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13098"/><hi type="bold">11. pulled away the shoulder--</hi>literally, "presented a refractory shoulder"; an image from beasts refusing to bear the yoke (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.29">Ne 9:29</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen24623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24624" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stopped ... ears--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Is 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.26">Jr 7:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.57">Ac 7:57</reference>). <div eID="gen24624" type="x-p"/>
entries.a84b3edc32846ff9201bc506de12f1be39342216: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13099"/><div sID="gen24625" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13099"/><hi type="bold">12. hearts ... adamant--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.9">Eze 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.19">11:19</reference>).<div eID="gen24625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord ... sent in Spirit by ... prophets--</hi>that is, sent by the former prophets inspired with His Spirit.<div eID="gen24626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24627" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore ... great wrath--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.16">2Ch 36:16</reference>). As they pushed from them the yoke of obedience, God laid on them the yoke of oppression. As they made their heart hard as adamant, God brake their hard hearts with judgments. Hard hearts must expect hard treatment. The harder the stone, the harder the blow of the hammer to break it. <div eID="gen24627" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e09102dd9f1d48070e35f7d101cca56cf891e48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13100"/><div sID="gen24628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13100"/><hi type="bold">13. he cried--</hi>by His prophets.<div eID="gen24628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they cried--</hi>in their calamities.<div eID="gen24629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ... not hear--</hi>retribution in kind (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.24-Prov.1.26">Pr 1:24-26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Is 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.4">Mi 3:4</reference>). <div eID="gen24630" type="x-p"/>
entries.6be0c3aa108ae76736cca100e73d32b1e4dd02a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13101"/><div sID="gen24631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13101"/><hi type="bold">14. whirlwind--</hi>of wrath (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.3">Na 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen24631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nations whom they knew not--</hi>foreign and barbarous.<div eID="gen24632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24633" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">desolate after them--</hi>after their expulsion and exile. It was ordered remarkably by God's providence, that no occupants took possession of it, but that during the Jews' absence it was reserved for them against their return after seventy years.<div eID="gen24633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they laid ... desolate--</hi>The Jews did so by their sins. The blame of their destruction lay with themselves, rather than with the Babylonians (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.21">2Ch 36:21</reference>).<div eID="gen24634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pleasant land--</hi>Canaan. Literally, "the land of desire" (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">Jr 3:19</reference>). <chapter eID="Zech.7"/>

entries.258997f64839177ab1d4e5372f8fc6664d663a92: <div eID="gen35552" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35553" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35554" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35554" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35553" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35555" type="x-p"/> Some Jews being sent from those who remained at Babylon to inquire of the priests and prophets at Jerusalem whether they were still bound to observe those fasts which had been appointed on occasion of the destruction of Jerusalem, and kept during the captivity, the prophet is commanded to take this opportunity of enforcing upon them the weightier matters of the law, judgment and mercy, that they might not incur such calamities as befell their fathers. He also intimates that in their former fasts they had regarded themselves more than God; and that they had rested too much on the performance of external rites, although the former prophets had largely insisted on the superior excellence of moral duties, <reference osisRef="Zac.7.1-Zac.7.14">Zac 7:1-14</reference>. <div eID="gen35555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35556" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35557" type="x-p"/> The fourth year of Ring Darius - Two years after they began to rebuild the temple, see <reference osisRef="Zac.1.1">Zac 1:1</reference>, A.M. 3486. <div eID="gen35557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35558" type="x-p"/> The ninth month, even in Chisleu - This answers to a part of our November and December. The names of the month appear only under and after the captivity.
entries.d182df604e022139f3fc194087c35852f9585a06: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35559" type="x-p"/> When they had sent - Sherezer and Regem-melech - To inquire whether the fasts should be continued, which they had hitherto observed on account of their ruined temple; and the reason why they inquired was, that they were rebuilding that temple, and were likely to bring it to a joyful issue.
entries.b627bc0b87cfda66ef4a011d9278df909a98a826: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35560" type="x-p"/> When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth - month - This they did in the remembrance of the burning of the temple, on the tenth day of that month; and on the seventh month, on the third of which month they observed a fast for the murder of Gedaliah, and the dispersion of the remnant of the people which were with him. See <reference osisRef="Jer.41.1">Jer 41:1</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.25">2Kgs 25:25</reference>.
entries.b8e453b8683df8bd1c53d1c0b7a28f544550eb19: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35561" type="x-p"/> And when ye did eat - They had not observed those fasts as they should have done. They deplored the loss of their temple, and its riches, etc., but they did not humble themselves because of those iniquities which had brought the displeasure of God upon them, their temple, and their city.
entries.2c860d9fe74d67da8c19ea58586bf5b82bda2c58: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen35561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35562" type="x-p"/> The words which the Lord hath cried by the former prophets - נביאים הראשנים nebiim harishonim, is the title which the Jews give to Joshua, Judges, the two books of Samuel, and the two books of Kings. <div eID="gen35562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35563" type="x-p"/> The latter prophets, נביאים אחרונים nebiim acharonim, are Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the twelve minor prophets. <div eID="gen35563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35564" type="x-p"/> The hagiographa, כתובים kethubim, holy writings, are the Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Song of Solomon, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and the two books of Chronicles. But the above words, the former prophets, seem to apply to Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. <div eID="gen35564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35565" type="x-p"/> The south and the plain? - From Eleutheropolis to the sea, <reference osisRef="Oba.1.19">Oba 1:19</reference>. The south was the wilderness and mountainous parts of Judea: and the plain, the plains of Jericho.
entries.5557e893ed59e63fd2086fcfbf7f6560fb45f955: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen35565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35566" type="x-p"/> Execute true judgment - See <reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">Isa 58:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">Isa 58:7</reference>; Jeremiah<reference osisRef="Jer.7.23">Jer 7:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.8">Mic 6:8</reference>, chap. 8.
entries.46d2e7a5691c9c65d26d86d5ff1d0fba50f1e667: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35567" type="x-p"/> Evil against his brother in your heart - Do not indulge an unfavourable opinion of another: do not envy him; do not harbour an unbrotherly feeling towards him.
entries.478960eaaba3498a15a152ac9fef2a73f36d63c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen35567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35568" type="x-p"/> Pulled away the shoulder - From under the yoke of the law, like an unbroken or restive bullock in the plough.
entries.5a2d2943ea626a495f6360c9aaf8ddf9924018aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35569" type="x-p"/> Made their hearts as an adamant stone - שמיר shamir may mean the granite. This is the hardest stone with which the common people could be acquainted. Perhaps the corundum, of which emery is a species, may be intended. Bochart thinks it means a stone used in polishing others. The same name, in Hebrew, applies to different stones.
entries.b5cf48ae53f4886dbe8159c4f68d4c2dbd182502: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen35569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35570" type="x-p"/> I scattered them with a whirlwind - This refers to the swift victories and cruel conduct of the Chaldeans towards the Jews; they came upon them like a whirlwind; they were tossed to and fro, and up and down, everywhere scattered and confounded.  <chapter eID="Zech.7"/> <div eID="gen35570" type="x-p"/>

entries.12b5a4f4c15c3034ace894f8a35088482434a7df: Zec 7:1-3 <div eID="gen16844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16845" type="x-p"/> Zec 7:1-3 describe the occasion for this instructive and consolatory “word of God,” which was addressed to Zechariah in the fourth year of Darius, i.e., two years after the building of the temple was resumed, and two years before its completion, and therefore at a time when the building must have been far advanced, and the temple itself was possibly already finished in the rough. Zec 7:1. <hi type="italic">“It came to pass in the fourth year of king Darius, that the word of Jehovah came to Zechariah, on the fourth (day) of the ninth month, in Kislev.” </hi> In this definition of the time we are surprised first of all at the circumstance, that, according to the Masoretic accentuation, and the division of the verses, the statement of the time is torn into two halves, and the notice of the year is placed after ויהי, whilst that of the month does not follow till after התה דבר יי; and secondly, at the fact that the introduction of the occurrence which led to this word of God is appended with the imperfect <hi type="italic">c. Vav rel.</hi> (<hi type="italic">vayyishlach</hi>), which would then stand in the sense of the pluperfect in opposition to the rule. On these grounds we must give up the Masoretic division of the verses, and connect the notice of the month and day in <hi type="italic">Zec 7:1</hi> with Zec 7:2, so that Zec 7:1 contains merely the general statement that in the fourth year of king Darius the word of the Lord came to Zechariah. What follows will then be appended thus: On the fourth day of the ninth month, in Kislev, Bethel sent, etc. Thus the more precise definition of the time is only given in connection with the following occurrence, because it was self-evident that the word of God which was addressed to the prophet in consequence of that event, could not have been addressed to him before it occurred. The rendering of the words in <hi type="italic">Zec 7:2</hi> is also a disputed point. We adopt the following: Zec 7:2. <hi type="italic">“Then Bethel sent Sharezer and Regem-melech, and his people, to entreat the face of Jehovah,</hi> (Zec 7:3) <hi type="italic">to speak to the priests who were at the house of Jehovah of hosts, and to the prophets, thus: Shall I weep, abstaining in the fifth month as I have now done so many years?” </hi> As <hi type="italic">Bēth</hi>-<hi type="italic">ēl</hi> may either signify the house of God, or be the name of the town of Bethel, it may be taken either as <hi type="italic">accus. loci</hi>, or as the subject of the sentence. Against the first explanation, which is very widely spread, viz., “it sent to the house of God, or to Bethel, Sharezer,” etc., or “they sent to the house of God Sharezer,” etc., it may be argued not only that the prophet, in order to make himself intelligible, ought either to have written <hi type="italic">'el Bēth</hi>-<hi type="italic">'ēl</hi>, or to have placed <hi type="italic">Bēth</hi>-<hi type="italic">'ēl</hi> after the object, but also that beeth-'eel cannot be shown to have been ever applied to the temple of Jehovah, and that it would have been altogether out of place to speak of sending to Bethel, because Jehovah could not be prayed to in Bethel after the captivity. We must therefore take <hi type="italic">bēth</hi>-<hi type="italic">'ēl</hi> as the subject, and understand it as denoting the population of Bethel, and not as a name given to the church of the Lord, since there are no conclusive passages to support any such use, as <hi type="italic">bēth Yehōvâh</hi> only is used for the church of God (see at Hos 8:1), and here there could be no inducement to employ so unusual an epithet to denote the nation. A considerable number of the earlier inhabitants of Bethel had already returned with Zerubbabel, according to Ezr 2:28 and <reference osisRef="Neh.7.32">Neh 7:32</reference>; and, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.11.31">Neh 11:31</reference>, the little town appears to have been soon rebuilt. The inhabitants of this city sent an embassy to Jerusalem, namely Sharezer and Rechem-Melech, and his men. The omission of the <hi type="italic">nota accus.</hi> את has indeed been adduced as an objection to this interpretation of the names as the object, and the names have been therefore taken as the subject, and regarded as in apposition to <hi type="italic">Bēth</hi>-<hi type="italic">ēl</hi>: “Bethel, namely Sharezer and Rechem, etc., sent;” that is to say, two men are mentioned in connection with Bethel, who are supposed to have acted as leaders of the embassy. But there is something so harsh and inflexible in the assumption of such an apposition as this, that in spite of the omission of the את we prefer to regard the names as accusatives. The name <hi type="italic">Sharezer</hi> is evidently Assyrian (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.37.38">Isa 37:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.3">Jer 39:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.13">Jer 39:13</reference>), so that the man was probably born in Babylonia. <div eID="gen16845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16846" type="x-p"/> The object of sending these men is given first of all in general terms: viz., להלּות את־פּני יי, lit., to stroke the face of Jehovah, - an anthropomorphic expression for affectionate entreaty (see at <reference osisRef="Ps.119.58">Psa 119:58</reference>), and then defined more precisely in Zec 7:3, where it is stated that they were to inquire of the priests and prophets, i.e., through their mediation, to entreat an answer from the Lord, whether the mourning and fasting were to be still kept up in the fifth month. Through the clause אשׁר לבית יי the priests are described as belonging to the house of Jehovah, though not in the sense supposed by Kliefoth, namely, “because they were appointed to serve in His house along with the Levites, in the place of the first-born, who were the possession of Jehovah” (Num 3:41; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.8-Deut.10.9">Deu 10:8-9</reference>). There is no such allusion here; but the meaning is simply, “as the persons in the temple, who by virtue of their mediatorial service were able to obtain an answer from Jehovah to a question addressed to Him in prayer.” The connection with the prophets points to this. The question האבכּה is defined by the inf. absol. הנּזר, as consisting in weeping or lamentation connected with abstinence from food and drink, i.e., with fasting. On this use of the <hi type="italic">inf. abs.</hi>, see Ewald, §280, <hi type="italic">a</hi>; הנּזר, to abstain (in this connection from meat and drink), is synonymous with צוּם in Zec 7:5. זה כּ מּה שׁנים: “these how many years,” for which we should say, “so many years.” <hi type="italic">Kammeh</hi> suggests the idea of an incalculably long duration. זה, in this and other similar combinations with numerical <hi type="italic">data</hi>, has acquired the force of an adverb: now, already (cf. Zec 1:12, and Ewald, §302, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). The subject to אבכּה is the population of Bethel, by which the men had been delegated. The question, however, had reference to a subject in which the whole community was interested, and hence the answer from God is addressed to all the people (Zec 7:5). So far as the circumstances themselves are concerned, we can see from Zec 7:5 and Zec 8:19, that during the captivity the Israelites had adopted the custom of commemorating the leading incidents in the Chaldaean catastrophe by keeping fast-days in the fifth, seventh, fourth, and tenth months. In the fifth month (<hi type="italic">Ab</hi>), on the tent day, because, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12-Jer.52.13">Jer 52:12-13</reference>, that was the day on which the temple and the city of Jerusalem were destroyed by fire in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, though the seventh day of that month is the date given in 2Ki 25:8-9 (see the comm. <hi type="italic">in loc.</hi>). In the seventh month, according to Jewish tradition, they fasted on the third day, on account of the murder of the governor Gedaliah, and the Judaeans who had been left in the land (2Ki 25:25-26; Jer 51:1.). In the fourth month <hi type="italic">Tammuz</hi>) they fasted on the ninth day, on account of the conquest of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar in the eleventh year of Zedekiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.2">Jer 39:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.6-Jer.52.7">Jer 52:6-7</reference>). And lastly, in the tenth month, a fast was kept on the tenth day on account of the commencement of the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar on that day, in the ninth year of Zedekiah (2Ki 25:1 and <reference osisRef="Jer.39.1">Jer 39:1</reference>).<note placement="foot">The later Jews kept the 9th Ab as the day when both the first and second temples were destroyed by fire; and in <hi type="italic">Mishna Taanit</hi> iv. 6, five disasters are enumerated, which had fallen upon Israel on that day: viz., (1) the determination of God not to suffer the fathers to enter the promised land; (2 and 3) the destruction of the first and second temples; (4) the conquest of the city of Bether in the time of <hi type="italic">Bar-Cochba</hi>; (5) the destruction of the holy city, which Rashi explains from Mic 3:12 and <reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">Jer 26:18</reference>, but which others refer to the fact that <hi type="italic">Turnus Rufus</hi> (either <hi type="italic">Turannius Rufus</hi> or <hi type="italic">T. Annius Rufus</hi>: cf. Schöttgen, <hi type="italic">Horae hebr. et talm.</hi> ii. 953ff., and Jost, <hi type="italic">Gesch. des Judenthums</hi>, ii. 77) ploughed over the foundation of the temple. Also, on the seventeenth of the fourth month (<hi type="italic">Tammuz</hi>), according to <hi type="italic">Mishna Taan.</hi> iv. 6, five disasters are said to have befallen Israel: (1) the breaking of the tables of the law (Exodus 32); (2) the cessation of the daily sacrifice in the first temple from the want of sacrificial lambs (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.52.6">Jer 52:6</reference>); (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.3">3</reference>) the breach made in the city walls; (4) the burning of the law by <hi type="italic">Apostemus</hi>; and (5) the setting up of the abomination, i.e., of an idol, in the temple (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.31">Dan 11:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.13">Dan 12:13</reference>). Vid., Lundius, <hi type="italic">Codex talm. de jejunio,</hi> Traf. ad Rhen. 1694, p. 55ff.; also in abstract in <hi type="italic">Mishna ed. Surenhus.</hi> ii. pp. 382-3.</note> <div eID="gen16846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16847" type="x-p"/> The question put by the delegates referred simply to the fasting in the fifth month, in commemoration of the destruction of the temple. And now that the rebuilding of the temple was rapidly approaching completion, it appeared no longer in character to continue to keep this day, especially as the prophets had proclaimed on the part of God, that the restoration of the temple would be a sign that Jehovah had once more restored His favour to the remnant of His people. If this fast-day were given up, the others would probably be also relinquished. The question actually involved the prayer that the Lord would continue permanently to bestow upon His people the favour which He had restored to them, and not only bring to completion the restoration of the holy place, which was already begun, but accomplish generally the glorification of Israel predicted by the earlier prophets. The answer given by the Lord through Zechariah to the people refers to this, since the priests and prophets could give no information in the matter of their own accord. <div eID="gen16847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16848" type="x-p"/> The answer from the Lord divides itself into two parts, Zec 7:4-14 and ch. 8. In the first part He explains what it is that He requires of the people, and why He has been obliged to punish them with exile: in the second He promises them the restoration of His favour and the promised salvation. Each of these parts is divisible again into two sections, Zec 7:4-7 and Zec 7:8-14; Zechariah 8:1-17 and Zec 8:18-23; and each of these sections opens with the formula, “The word of Jehovah (of hosts) came to me (Zechariah), saying.”
entries.306e55b6e382e2128b8d2f1b2ab69daff1b2d7f4: Zec 7:4-7 <div eID="gen16848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16849" type="x-p"/> The first of these four words of God contains an exposure of what might be unwarrantable in the question and its motives, and open to disapproval. Zec 7:4. <hi type="italic">“And the word of Jehovah of hosts came to me thus,</hi> Zec 7:5. <hi type="italic">Speak to all the people of the land, and to the priests, saying, When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and in the seventh (month), and that for seventy years, did ye, when fasting, fast to me?</hi> Zec 7:6. <hi type="italic">And when ye eat, and when ye drink, is it not ye who eat, and ye who drink?</hi> Zec 7:7. <hi type="italic">Does it not concern the words, which Jehovah has preached through the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and satisfied, and her towns round about her, and the south country and the low land were inhabited?” </hi> The thought of Zec 7:6 and Zec 7:7 is the following: It is a matter of indifference to God whether the people fast or not. The true fasting, which is well pleasing to God, consists not in a pharisaical abstinence from eating and drinking, but in the fact that men observe the word of God and live thereby, as the prophets before the captivity had already preached to the people. This overthrew the notion that men could acquire the favour of God by fasting, and left it to the people to decide whether they would any longer observe the previous fast-days; it also showed what God would require of them if they wished to obtain the promised blessings. For the inf. absol. see at Hag 1:6. The fasting in the seventh month was not the fast on the day of atonement which was prescribed in the law (Leviticus 23), but, as has been already observed, the fast in commemoration of the murder of Gedaliah. In the form צמתּני the suffix is not a substitute for the dative (Ges. §121, 4), but is to be taken as an accusative, expressive of the fact that the fasting related to God (Ewald, §315, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). The suffix is strengthened by אני for the sake of emphasis (Ges. §121, 3). In Zec 7:7 the form of the sentence is elliptical. The verb is omitted in the clause הלוא את־הדּברים, but not the subject, say זה, which many commentators supply, after the lxx, the Peshito, and the Vulgate (“Are these not the words which Jehovah announced?”), in which case את would have to be taken as <hi type="italic">nota nominativi</hi>. The sentence contains an <hi type="italic">aposiopesis</hi>, and is to be completed by supplying a verb, either “should ye not do or give heed to the words which,” etc.? or “do ye not know the words?” ישׁבת, as in Zec 1:11, in the sense of sitting or dwelling; not in a passive sense, “to be inhabited,” although it might be so expressed. שׁלוה is synonymous with שׁקטת in Zec 1:11. ישׁב, in the sense indicated at the close of the verse, is construed in the singular masculine, although it refers to a plurality of previous nouns (cf. Ges. §148, 2). In addition to Jerusalem, the following are mentioned as a periphrasis for the land of Judah: (1) her towns round about; these are the towns belonging to Jerusalem as the capital, towns of the mountains of Judah which were more or less dependent upon her: (2) the two rural districts, which also belonged to the kingdom of Judah, viz., the <hi type="italic">negeb</hi>, the south country (which Koehler erroneously identifies with the mountains of Judah; compare <reference osisRef="Josh.15.21">Jos 15:21</reference> with <reference osisRef="Josh.15.48">Jos 15:48</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">shephēlâh</hi>, or lowland along the coast of the Mediterranean (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.33">Jos 15:33</reference>).
entries.235fa3ebedb94774e1007bf6165671f9b2e159f8: Zec 7:8-12 <div eID="gen16849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16850" type="x-p"/> The second word of the Lord recals to the recollection of the people the disobedience of the fathers, and its consequences, viz., the judgment of exile, as a warning example. The introduction of the prophet’s name in the heading in Zec 7:8 does not warrant the strange opinion held by Schmieder and Schlier - namely, that our prophet is here reproducing the words of an earlier Zechariah who lived before the captivity - but is merely to be attributed to a variation in the form of expression. This divine word was as follows: Zec 7:9. <hi type="italic">“Thus hath Jehovah of hosts spoken, saying, Execute judgment of truth, and show love and compassion one to another.</hi> Zec 7:10. <hi type="italic">And widows and orphans, strangers and destitute ones, oppress not; and meditate not in your heart the injury of every brother.</hi> Zec 7:11. <hi type="italic">But they refused to attend, and offered a rebellious shoulder, and hardened their ears that they might not hear.</hi> Zec 7:12. <hi type="italic">And they made their heart diamond, that they might not hear the law and the words which Jehovah of hosts sent through His Spirit by means of the former prophet, so that great wrath came from Jehovah of hosts.” </hi>כּה אמר is to be taken as a preterite here, referring to what Jehovah had caused to be proclaimed to the people before the captivity. The kernel of this announcement consisted in the appeal to the people, to keep the moral precepts of the law, to practise the true love of the neighbour in public life and private intercourse. <hi type="italic">Mishpat 'ĕmeth</hi>, judgment of truth (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.8">Eze 18:8</reference>), is such an administration of justice as simply fixes the eye upon the real circumstances of any dispute, without any personal considerations whatever, and decides them in accordance with truth. For the fact itself, compare <reference osisRef="Exod.22.20">Exo 22:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.21">Exo 22:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.6-Exod.23.9">Exo 23:6-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.19.15-Lev.19.18">Lev 19:15-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.18-Deut.10.19">Deu 10:18-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.24.14">Deu 24:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.17">Isa 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.5-Jer.7.6">Jer 7:5-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.3">Jer 22:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.8">Eze 18:8</reference>; Hos 12:7, etc. רעת אישׁ אחיו, the injury of a man who is his brother (as in <reference osisRef="Gen.9.5">Gen 9:5</reference>); not “injury one towards another,” which would suppose a transposition of the אישׁ = אישׁ רעת אחיו. In Zec 7:11, Zec 7:12 the attitude of the people towards these admonitions of God is described. <hi type="italic">Nâthan kâthēph sōrereth</hi>: to give or offer a rebellious shoulder, as in Neh 9:29. The figure is borrowed from an ox, which will not allow a yoke to be placed upon its neck (cf. Hos 4:16). To make the ears heavy (<hi type="italic">hikhbı̄d</hi>), away from hearing, i.e., so that they do not hear (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Isa 6:10</reference>). To make the heart diamond (<hi type="italic">shâmı̄r</hi>), i.e., as hard as diamond. A stony heart is a heart not susceptible to impressions (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.19">Eze 11:19</reference>). The relative אשׁר before <hi type="italic">shâlach</hi> refers to the two nouns named before, viz., <hi type="italic">tōrâh</hi> and <hi type="italic">debhârı̄m</hi>, though we need not on that account take <hi type="italic">tōrâh</hi> in the general sense of instruction. God also sent the law to the people through the prophets, i.e., caused them to preach it and impress it upon their hearts. The consequence of this obduracy of the people was, that “there arose great wrath from Jehovah” (cf. Zec 1:2; 2Ki 3:27).
entries.a9279b801c6b479c31380456620308cae06b3fb8: Zec 7:13-14 <div eID="gen16850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16851" type="x-p"/> This wrath is described in Zec 7:13, Zec 7:14. Zec 7:13. <hi type="italic">“It came to pass: as he cried and they did not hear, so will they cry and I shall not hear, said Jehovah of hosts.</hi> Zec 7:14. <hi type="italic">And I will scatter them with a whirlwind over all nations, who did not know them, and the land is laid waste behind them, so that no one passes to and fro. And thus they made the choice land a desert.” </hi> The form of the address changes in Zec 7:13. Whereas in the protasis the prophet is still speaking of Jehovah in the third person, in the apodosis he introduces Jehovah as speaking (so will they cry, and I, etc.) and announcing the punishment, which He will inflict upon the rebellious and has already inflicted in their captivity. This address of God is continued in Zec 7:14 as far as וּמשּׁב. The opinion, that the address terminates with לא ידעוּם, and that והארץ commences the account of the accomplishment of the purpose to punish, is not so much at variance with the circumstance, that in that case the last two clauses of Zec 7:14 would say essentially the same thing, as with the fact that והארץ וגו cannot, from its very form, be taken as an account of the accomplishment of the divine purpose. The perfect <hi type="italic">nâshammâh</hi> in this clause does not preclude our connecting it with the preceding one, but is used to set forth the devastation as a completed fact: the land will be (not become) waste. The infliction of the punishment is expressed in Zec 7:13 in the form of a divine <hi type="italic">talio</hi>. As they have not hearkened to the word of God, so will God, when they call upon Him, namely in distress (cf. Hos 5:15), also not hear (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.11.11">Jer 11:11</reference>), but whirl them like a tempest over the nations. The form אסערם is the first pers. imperf. <hi type="italic">piel</hi> for אסערם or אסערם, and Aramaic (cf. Ges. §52, 2, Anm. 2). On the nations whom they do not know, and who will therefore have no pity and compassion upon them, compare <reference osisRef="Jer.22.28">Jer 22:28</reference>; Jer 16:13. מעבר וּמשּׁב (cf. Zec 9:8), that not one goes to and fro in the desolate land; lit., goes away from a place and returns again (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.32.27">Exo 32:27</reference>). In the clause ויּשׂימוּ וגו the result of the stiff-necked obstinacy of the fathers is briefly stated: They have made the choice land a desert (<hi type="italic">'erets chemdâh</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">Jer 3:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.106.24">Psa 106:24</reference>), so that they have brought upon the land all the calamity which is now bewailed upon the fast-days. Renewal and Completion of the Covenant of Grace - Zechariah 8 <div eID="gen16851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16852" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have the second half of the Lord’s answer to the question concerning the last-days, which promises to the people the restitution of the former relation of grace, and the future glorification of Israel, on the simple condition of their observing the moral precepts of the law. This double promise is contained in two words of God, each of which is divided into a number of separate sayings, containing the separate details of the salvation bestowed by the formula כּה אמר יי צ (thus saith Jehovah of hosts): the first into seven (Zec 8:2, Zec 8:3, Zec 8:4-5, Zec 8:6, Zec 8:7, Zec 8:9, Zec 8:14-17), the second into three (Zec 8:19, Zec 8:20-22, and Zec 8:23). Jerome observes, with reference to this: “By the separate words and sentences, in which Israel is promised not only prosperity, but things almost incredible in their magnitude, the prophet declares, 'Thus saith the Almighty God;' saying, in other words, Do not imagine that the things which I promise are my own, and so disbelieve me as only a man; they are the promises of God which I unfold.”  <chapter eID="Zech.7"/> <div eID="gen16852" type="x-p"/>

entries.3b5d64cfd27d2dc831906b83aa9a678761196417:
Chapter 7
Lecture One Hundred and Forty-sixth
Zechariah 7:1-3
1. And it came to pass in the fourth year of king Darius, that the word of the LORD came unto Zechariah in the fourth day of the ninth month, even in Chisleu;
1. Et factus est (datus est,) anno quarto Darii regis, sermo Iehovae ad Zachariam, quarta die mensis noni Chisleu;
2. When they had sent unto the house of God Sherezer and Regemmelech, and their men, to pray before the LORD,
2. Nam miserat in domum Dei (hoc est, Templum) Sareezer et Regem-melech et viros ejus ad deprecandam faciem Iehovae (aut, Miserat in domum Dei Sareezer et Regem-melech, in nominativo casu, et viri ejus ad deprecandam faciem Iehovae:)
3. And to speak unto the priests which were in the house of the LORD of hosts, and to the prophets, saying, Should I weep in the fifth month, separating myself, as I have done these so many years?
